newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Seguin, scenting power, embraces euro.
newsitem.headline: France's Seguin, scenting power, embraces euro.

text.p: Philippe Seguin, France's Gaullist National Assembly speaker, scenting an outside chance of winning the premiership, is on his best behaviour.

The heavyweight orator, who led the "no" campaign in a 1992 referendum on the Maastricht treaty on European union, has shifted closer to President Jacques Chirac's drive for a single European currency as he senses a possible breakthrough.

Seguin has toned down his anti-Maastricht rhetoric as polls show he is the most popular candidate to succeed unpopular Prime Minister Alain Juppe if the centre-right retains power by a narrow majority in the May 25-June 1 parliamentary election.

The 54-year-old former social affairs minister has refrained from endorsing Juppe's austerity policies and called instead for a review of the Maastricht budget criteria, and for European Union policy to be geared more towards creating jobs.

But campaign statements such as "We must certainly launch the single European currency; the French people have so decided" stand in marked contrast to a book published just a year ago in which he called the euro "the false prophets' new Holy Grail".

Seguin's social Gaullism, with its emphasis on the role of the state in protecting the weak and jobless, has been a useful counterfoil at the hustings to the Juppe government's record of austerity, tax increases and record unemployment.
Seguin has also sought to distance himself from state economic "dirigisme" saying he supports "a tempered liberalism".
But European partners and financial markets may wonder how far the anti-Maastricht leopard has really changed his spots.

Asked about his chances of becoming prime minister, Seguin told a television interviewer on Sunday: "Occupying a position just for the pleasure of occupying it at the price of forgetting my own ideas is not my style."
Political sources say Chirac may have serious misgivings about promoting a man of such political unpredictability, robust temper and presidential ambition.

Seguin defied the leadership of his Gaullist RPR party and came within a whisker of turning voters against EU economic and monetary union in a 1992 referendum on the Maastricht treaty. The majority for the treaty was just 51.05 percent.
An outstanding orator, Seguin was chosen to represent the anti-Maastricht camp in a crucial live television debate with Socialist president Francois Mitterrand who was ill with cancer.
He chose to be respectful rather than confrontational, disappointing some of his supporters but earning others' respect for statesmanship.
Hoping to silence him with a largely ceremonial job, the RPR had Seguin elected assembly president in 1993 after emerging as the biggest party in a parliamentary election.
Instead, the rebel became an authoritarian and active speaker, trying to build up the Assembly's role, punishing absenteeism and reforming the parliamentary calendar.
His huge bearlike figure and deep voice became familiar to viewers as he scolded deputies like schoolchildren for rumpus in the twice-weekly televised question time.

He used his high-profile position to become the social conscience of Chirac's centre-right coalition, accusing then Gaullist prime minister Edouard Balladur of capitulating to unemployment and comparing his policies to the Western powers' appeasement of Hitler during World War Two.

When Chirac was elected president and appointed Juppe as prime minister, Seguin continued to warn that indiscriminate budget cuts would not pull France out of recession and advocated a more expansionary economic policy.
The personal rivalry with Juppe is palpable whenever the two men are together, aides say.

The popular satirical television show Les Guignols depicted him in the speaker's chair behind and above Juppe, taunting the infuriated premier by repeating "It won't work" as he outlined his platform to the assembly.

Born in Tunis in 1943, Seguin never knew his father, who was killed in World War Two when he was a baby. He graduated from the elite civil service school Ecole Nationale d'Administration and joined the private office of centrist prime minister Raymond Barre in 1977.
He has been a member of parliament for the eastern town of Epinal since 1978 and is also mayor of Epinal.
He was a popular minister for social affairs in 1986-88, when conservatives returned to power in the first experiment in left-right "cohabitation" with Mitterrand.
